questions.e: Lost or stolen keys break the protection that encryption provides.

questions.q: In security zones, what is the difference between trusted and untrusted?
o: Trusted is the internal network you control; untrusted is outside it, such as the internet
questions.e: Firewalls control traffic between zones, with the screened subnet in between.

questions.q: A switch port in a public reception area isn't used. What should you do?
o: Disable it (administratively shut it down) or put it in an unused VLAN
questions.e: Unused live ports let anyone plug in.

questions.q: A new firewall rule allows HTTPS to a web server but users still can't connect. The first rule in the list denies all traffic from the internet. What is the problem?
o: Rule order: the deny rule matches first, so the allow rule is never reached
questions.e: Move the specific allow rule above the broad deny.

questions.q: Which is the most secure way to manage a switch remotely?
o: SSH with strong credentials, limited to a management network
questions.e: Combine encrypted protocols with access restrictions and logging.

questions.q: Which device should sit in the screened subnet?
questions.e: Only systems that must be reachable from the internet belong there.

questions.q: What does content filtering add beyond URL filtering?
o: It inspects the actual content of pages or files, not just the address
questions.e: For example, blocking certain file types or keywords.

questions.q: Which statement about ACLs is correct?
o: They can filter by source and destination IP, port and protocol
They only filter by MAC address
They can't be used on routers
questions.e: ACLs are used on routers, firewalls and Layer 3 switches.

questions.q: A company wants every device to prove it has up-to-date antivirus before joining the wired network. What should it deploy?
questions.e: NAC can check device health as well as identity.

questions.q: Why should default SNMP community strings be changed or SNMPv3 used?
o: Defaults like 'public' are widely known and let attackers read or change device settings
questions.e: Default credentials are one of the first things attackers try.

questions.q: What is the first step of the CompTIA troubleshooting methodology?
o: Establish a theory of probable cause
questions.e: Gather information, question users, identify symptoms, find out what changed and duplicate the problem if possible.

questions.q: Which step comes straight after establishing a theory of probable cause?
o: Test the theory to determine the cause
questions.e: If the test doesn't confirm the theory, set up a new theory or escalate.

questions.q: What should you do if testing doesn't confirm your theory?
o: Establish a new theory or escalate
questions.e: Don't make changes based on an unproven theory.

questions.q: What is the final step of the methodology?
o: Document findings, actions, outcomes and lessons learned
questions.e: Documentation helps the next person who sees the same problem.

questions.q: Which step includes implementing preventive measures, if applicable?
questions.e: After fixing it, confirm everything works and take steps to stop it happening again.

questions.q: Which step includes considering multiple approaches such as top-to-bottom or bottom-to-top OSI?
o: Establish a theory of probable cause
questions.e: Divide and conquer, top-down and bottom-up are ways of working through possible causes.

questions.q: Several users report different problems at the same time. What does the methodology recommend?
o: Fix them all with one change
questions.e: Tackling problems one by one avoids confusing cause and effect.

questions.q: A user says the network 'stopped working after lunch'. What is a key question to ask during problem identification?
questions.e: Recent changes are a common cause. Check change logs too.

questions.q: What should you do before implementing a fix that could affect many users?
o: Establish a plan of action, considering the impact and change management
questions.e: Plans include rollback steps and scheduling to limit disruption.

questions.q: Which approach starts at Layer 1 and works up the OSI model?
questions.e: Bottom-up suits problems likely to be physical, such as no link light.

questions.q: Which approach starts in the middle of the OSI model, for example with a ping, then moves up or down depending on the result?
questions.e: A successful ping rules out Layers 1 to 3 quickly.

questions.q: Why try to duplicate the problem?
o: To see the symptoms for yourself and confirm what's happening
questions.e: Reproducing a fault helps confirm the cause and later the fix.

questions.q: When should you escalate a problem?
o: When it's beyond your knowledge, access or authority, or your theories have been ruled out
questions.e: Escalating follows the methodology, so don't see it as a failure.

questions.q: After applying a fix for one user, what should you do before closing the ticket?
o: Verify full system functionality with the user
questions.e: Make sure the fix worked and didn't break something else.

questions.q: Which step is 'question the obvious'?
o: Establish a theory of probable cause
questions.e: Check simple things first: is it plugged in, powered on and connected?

questions.q: Long Ethernet runs near fluorescent lights and motors show many errors. What is the likely cause?
questions.e: Re-route the cable or use shielded cable.

questions.q: What is crosstalk?
o: Signal from one wire pair bleeding into another
questions.e: Poor terminations that untwist too much wire increase crosstalk (NEXT and FEXT).

questions.q: What is attenuation?
o: Loss of signal strength over distance
questions.e: Copper and fibre both lose signal with length, which is why distance limits exist.

questions.q: Which interface counter shows frames smaller than 64 bytes?
questions.e: Runts often come from collisions or a duplex mismatch.

questions.q: Which interface counter shows frames larger than the allowed MTU?
questions.e: Giants can appear with an MTU mismatch, such as one side using jumbo frames.

questions.q: An interface shows a rising number of CRC errors. What is a likely cause?
o: A damaged cable, bad termination or interference
questions.e: CRC errors mean frames arrived corrupted, usually a physical problem.

questions.q: A switch port shows 'administratively down'. What does that mean?
o: Someone has disabled it with a shutdown command
questions.e: Enable it with 'no shutdown' if it should be in use.

questions.q: A switch port shows 'err-disabled'. What is a common reason?
o: A security feature such as port security or BPDU guard shut it down
questions.e: Fix the cause, then reset the port.

questions.q: A new access point won't power up on a PoE switch, although other APs work. What should you check?
o: Whether the switch's PoE budget is used up, and whether the AP needs PoE+ or PoE++
questions.e: Each switch has a total PoE budget, and devices need a matching PoE standard.

questions.q: Which PoE standard provides up to 30 W per port (PoE+)?
questions.e: 802.3af is about 15.4 W, 802.3at about 30 W and 802.3bt up to 60 or 90 W.

questions.q: A fibre link won't come up. One end uses a single-mode transceiver and the other multimode. What is the problem?
questions.e: Transceivers, fibre type and wavelengths must match at both ends.

questions.q: A newly installed fibre link has no light. The cable is fine. What is a common simple mistake?
o: The TX and RX strands are swapped (transposed)
questions.e: TX on one end must reach RX on the other.

questions.q: A fibre link is up but with errors, and the received light level is very low. What should you check?
o: Dirty connectors, bends or damage, and whether the run is too long
questions.e: Clean connectors and check the signal strength (dB loss) against the transceiver's spec.

questions.q: A 10 Gbps link is running over Cat 5e cable for 80 metres and drops to 1 Gbps. Why?
o: Cat 5e isn't rated for 10 Gbps; Cat 6a is needed for 10 Gbps at that length
questions.e: Using the wrong cable category limits speed.

questions.q: A technician terminates a cable but untwists 5 cm of each pair. What problem might this cause?
o: Crosstalk and errors from improper termination
questions.e: Keep pairs twisted as close to the connector as possible.

questions.q: A link shows high output drops. What does that usually mean?
o: The interface is congested and its buffers are overflowing
questions.e: Drops point to more traffic than the link can carry.

questions.q: Using multimode fibre with single-mode transceivers over a long run would cause:
o: Signal problems or no link, because fibre types must match
questions.e: Always match the cable type to the transceiver.

questions.q: A port shows as 'suspended' on a link aggregation group. What is likely?
o: That member's settings don't match the bundle, so it was suspended
The cable is fine and it's forwarding
questions.e: All members need matching speed, duplex and VLAN settings.

questions.q: Which tool would quickly tell you if a copper cable has an open wire or a short?
questions.e: Cable testers check continuity and wiring order.

questions.q: Two old switches, neither supporting auto-MDIX, are connected with a straight-through cable. What happens?
o: No link, because TX and RX aren't crossed
questions.e: Use a crossover cable or a switch that supports auto-MDIX.

questions.q: Users suddenly report the whole network is extremely slow, and switch CPUs are at 100% with huge broadcast traffic. What is likely?
o: A duplex mismatch on one PC
questions.e: Loops cause broadcast storms. Check spanning tree and recent cabling changes.

questions.q: A PC in VLAN 10 is plugged into a port configured for VLAN 20. What will happen?
o: It gets the wrong subnet (or no DHCP) and can't reach its normal resources
questions.e: Check the port's VLAN assignment against the documentation.

questions.q: A user can reach local resources but nothing outside the subnet. What is a likely cause?
questions.e: Without a correct gateway, traffic can't leave the subnet.

questions.q: Users can reach sites by IP address but not by name. What is likely?
questions.e: Check the DNS server settings and whether the server responds.

questions.q: New devices are getting APIPA addresses while existing ones work. What is a likely cause?
o: The DHCP scope has run out of addresses (pool exhaustion)
questions.e: Shorten the lease time, enlarge the scope or tidy up old leases.

questions.q: A PC shows a 'duplicate IP address' warning. What has happened?
o: Another device is already using the same IP, often due to a static address inside the DHCP range
questions.e: Exclude static addresses from the DHCP scope.

questions.q: A user has IP 192.168.1.50 with mask 255.255.0.0 while everyone else uses 255.255.255.0. What problem might this cause?
o: Wrong subnet mask, so the PC misjudges which hosts are local
questions.e: The /16 mask makes the PC treat any 192.168.x.x host as local, so it ARPs for them instead of sending traffic to the gateway.

questions.q: Traffic to a server is blocked after a firewall change, but only for one subnet. What should you check first?
o: The ACL rules added in the change
questions.e: Misconfigured ACLs often block more than intended.

questions.q: A router can't reach the internet, and 'show ip route' shows no 0.0.0.0/0 entry. What is missing?
questions.e: Without a default route, packets for unknown networks are dropped.

questions.q: Why might the wrong switch become the STP root bridge?
o: The priority wasn't set, so an old switch with a lower MAC address won the election
questions.e: Set the root priority deliberately on a core switch.

questions.q: Which STP port role is the best path towards the root bridge on a non-root switch?
questions.e: Each non-root switch has one root port. Designated ports forward away from the root.

questions.q: Wi-Fi users drop off when walking between two APs. What could cause this?
o: Poor roaming due to coverage gaps or AP settings
questions.e: Check overlap between APs, signal strength and roaming features.

questions.q: Neighbouring APs are all on channel 1 and users report slow Wi-Fi. What is the issue?
questions.e: Spread APs across 1, 6 and 11 on 2.4 GHz, or use 5 GHz.

questions.q: Users far from an AP get a weak signal and slow speeds. What is this?
o: Signal loss due to distance and obstacles
questions.e: Add APs, reposition them or change antennas based on a site survey.

questions.q: A client keeps disconnecting from Wi-Fi without moving. What should you investigate?
o: Interference, signal strength and disassociation events, including possible deauthentication attacks
questions.e: Disassociation can be caused by interference, AP settings or an attacker.

questions.q: Microwave ovens in the staff kitchen disrupt Wi-Fi at lunch. Which band is affected?
questions.e: Microwaves operate around 2.4 GHz. Moving clients to 5 GHz helps.

questions.q: A switch port has the wrong native VLAN on one end of a trunk. What may happen?
o: Untagged traffic leaks into the wrong VLAN and CDP/LLDP may log a native VLAN mismatch
questions.e: Native VLANs must match on both ends of a trunk.

questions.q: Wi-Fi works but a site visitor can't reach the internet on guest Wi-Fi until they open a browser. Why?
o: A captive portal needs them to accept terms or log in first
questions.e: Captive portals intercept the first web request.

questions.q: What is a common fix for DHCP address pool exhaustion on a busy guest network?
o: Reduce the lease time and/or enlarge the scope
Increase the lease time to 30 days
questions.e: Short leases free addresses from devices that have left.

questions.q: Two routers keep passing packets back and forth for one destination, and traceroute shows the same hops repeating. What is this?
questions.e: Check static routes and routing protocol configuration. TTL eventually drops the packets.

questions.q: Which STP port state forwards traffic normally?
questions.e: Ports pass through listening and learning before forwarding in classic STP.

questions.q: What is jitter?
o: Variation in packet delay, which makes voice and video choppy
questions.e: QoS and enough bandwidth help keep jitter low.

questions.q: What is latency?
o: The time it takes data to travel from source to destination
questions.e: High latency makes interactive applications feel slow.

questions.q: What is the difference between bandwidth and throughput?
o: Bandwidth is the link's capacity; throughput is the data actually delivered
questions.e: Throughput is lower due to overhead, congestion and errors.

questions.q: What is a bottleneck?
o: The slowest point in a path that limits overall performance
questions.e: For example, a 1 Gbps uplink serving many 1 Gbps users.

questions.q: Many users share a single 1 Gbps uplink and it runs at 100% at peak times. What is this?
questions.e: Upgrade the link, add link aggregation or apply QoS.

questions.q: Video calls freeze and have missing sound. Monitoring shows 5% packet loss. What should you look at?
o: Packet loss causes, such as congestion, errors on a link or Wi-Fi interference
questions.e: Real-time apps cope badly with even small amounts of loss.

questions.q: Which is most sensitive to jitter and latency?
questions.e: Interactive real-time traffic needs consistent, low delay.

questions.q: A satellite link has high latency even when lightly used. Why?
o: The signal travels a very long distance to and from the satellite
questions.e: Geostationary satellites add hundreds of milliseconds of delay.

questions.q: A file transfer is slow on a 1 Gbps link. Interface counters show many CRC errors. What is the likely cause of poor throughput?
questions.e: Errors mean resending data, which cuts throughput.

questions.q: Which tool helps confirm the actual throughput a user is getting?
o: A speed tester or throughput test tool
questions.e: Compare results against expected speeds and baselines.

questions.q: Which technique prioritises VoIP during congestion?
questions.e: QoS marks and queues traffic so time-sensitive packets go first.

questions.q: A Wi-Fi network slows when 60 people join a meeting room AP at once. What is the main cause?
o: Too many clients contending for the same AP's airtime
questions.e: Add APs for high-density areas and use 5 or 6 GHz.

questions.q: Why is device uptime a useful performance metric?
o: It shows reliability and whether a device has restarted unexpectedly
questions.e: Unexpected reboots can explain intermittent problems.

questions.q: Users on public hotspot Wi-Fi get slow speeds and pages that won't load until they log in. What explains the login part?
o: The hotspot uses a captive portal
questions.e: Until the portal is completed, most traffic is blocked or redirected.

questions.q: What does packet loss mean?
o: Some packets never arrive at their destination
questions.e: Causes include congestion, errors and interference.

questions.q: Which command tests basic reachability to another host?
questions.e: Ping sends ICMP echo requests. No reply doesn't always mean the host is down, as ICMP may be blocked.

questions.q: Which command shows each router hop on the path to a destination on Windows?
questions.e: Windows uses tracert. Linux and macOS use traceroute.

questions.q: Which tools query DNS records directly?
questions.e: dig is common on Linux and macOS. nslookup is on Windows and Linux.

questions.q: Which command shows active connections and listening ports on a computer?
questions.e: Useful for spotting unexpected services or connections.

questions.q: Which command shows the IP configuration on a Windows PC?
questions.e: Linux uses 'ip addr' (or the older ifconfig).

questions.q: Which command shows the IP to MAC address mappings a computer has learned?
questions.e: Useful for spotting duplicate IPs or ARP spoofing.

questions.q: What does Nmap do?
o: Scans hosts to find open ports, services and sometimes operating systems
questions.e: Only scan networks you're authorised to test.

questions.q: What does tcpdump do?
o: Captures packets from the command line, usually on Linux
questions.e: Captures can be opened in a protocol analyser such as Wireshark.

questions.q: What is a protocol analyser such as Wireshark used for?
o: Capturing and decoding network traffic to see exactly what's happening
questions.e: It shows each packet's headers and contents.

questions.q: What do LLDP and CDP show?
o: Information about directly connected neighbouring devices, such as their name, port and model
questions.e: LLDP is the open standard. CDP is Cisco's protocol.

questions.q: Which hardware tool finds which wall jack a cable in a bundle connects to?
questions.e: The toner puts a signal on the cable and the probe picks it up at the other end.

questions.q: Which tool shines visible red light down a fibre to find breaks or sharp bends?
questions.e: Light escapes at the fault and can be seen.

questions.q: Which tool shows nearby wireless networks, channels and signal strengths?
questions.e: Use it to pick clear channels and find interference.

questions.q: What is a network tap?
o: A hardware device that copies traffic from a link for monitoring
questions.e: Taps give a full copy of traffic, unlike some mirror ports that may drop frames under load.

questions.q: Which switch command shows which MAC addresses have been learned on which ports?
questions.e: Useful for finding which port a device is plugged into. Older IOS versions and the objectives write it as show mac-address-table.

questions.q: Which switch command shows each port's VLAN membership?
questions.e: Check this when a device is on the wrong network.

questions.q: Which device command shows PoE power use per port?
questions.e: Helps diagnose PoE budget problems.

questions.q: Which command shows a device's interface status, errors and counters?
questions.e: Look for errors, drops, duplex and speed.

questions.q: Which command displays a device's running configuration?
questions.e: Compare it with the saved and golden configs.

questions.q: A user can't reach a server. Ping by IP works but nslookup fails. What should you check?
questions.e: Ping working rules out basic connectivity.

questions.q: Which Linux command shows interface addresses on modern systems?
questions.e: ifconfig is older and may not be installed by default.

questions.q: Which hardware tool checks whether a wired cable meets its rated performance, such as for Cat 6?
questions.e: Basic testers check wiring. Certifiers test performance against the standard.

questions.q: A traceroute stops responding after the third hop. What does this suggest?
o: A problem at or after that hop, or a device there blocking ICMP
questions.e: Some routers don't reply to traceroute, so check further before assuming a fault.

questions.q: Which tool shows a device's route table on Windows?
questions.e: Linux uses 'ip route' or 'route -n'.
